cards.text: Paul has been locked up in Caesarea for two years, and now there's a new governor: Porcius Festus, who took over from Felix (Acts 24:27). Just three days after Festus arrives in the province, he goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. THREE DAYS in and he's already on the road, friend, when three days into a new job I'm still asking where they keep the cookie sheets.

cards.question: Festus has just arrived in Jerusalem. Who presents a case against Paul to him there?

answers.text: The chief priests and Jewish leaders

cards.text: They urge Festus to grant them a concession against Paul by summoning him to Jerusalem. Sounds like a simple favor, but friend, it is NOT a simple favor.

cards.question: Why do the leaders want Festus to summon Paul from Caesarea to Jerusalem?

answers.text: To ambush and kill him on the way
To have him speak at the temple
To let the high priest question him

cards.question: The leaders ask Festus to bring Paul to Jerusalem. Festus agrees to do it.

cards.text: Festus tells them Paul is being held in Caesarea and he's going there soon himself, so some of their leaders can come down with him and accuse Paul there. Somebody's got to go tell the ambush crew the plans changed.
Festus spends no more than eight or ten days with them in Jerusalem. Then he heads back down to Caesarea.

cards.question: Festus is back in Caesarea. He sits on the judgment seat the ___ day and orders that Paul be brought in.

cards.text: Paul is brought in, and the Jews who came down from Jerusalem stand all around him, bringing many serious charges. Friend, if that many people circled me and pointed, I'd confess to stealing cookies I never even baked.

cards.question: The accusers from Jerusalem are able to prove the serious charges they bring against Paul.
Surrounded by his accusers, Paul makes his defense. What does Paul tell Festus?

answers.text: He broke a minor temple rule

cards.text: But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, asks Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?” Jerusalem. Paul, the baker and I all just heard about that ambush, and I'm sitting here going, NO, NO, NO.

cards.question: Festus asks Paul to go up to Jerusalem for trial. Where does Paul say he ought to be tried?
Paul tells Festus he has done nothing wrong to the Jews, as Festus himself ___ very well.

cards.text: Then Paul says if he's guilty of anything worthy of death, he doesn't refuse to die, but if there's no truth to the accusations, no one has the right to hand him over to them. Friend, that is not a man ducking anything.

cards.question: Paul says no one has the right to hand him over to his accusers. What does Paul do next?

answers.text: He asks for Lysias the commander

cards.question: Festus confers with his council, then turns down Paul's appeal to Caesar.

cards.text: Festus tells Paul, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!” And that's where we stop for now, friend, because Paul's story is NOT finished.

findings.problem: The blank is 'next' in 'the ___ day.' It is a minor time detail the baker has never seen and has no way to reason out from the earlier cards, so picking it comes down to luck. The question tests wording, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The joke 'I'd confess to stealing cookies I never even baked' doesn't click. Taking cookies someone else baked is ordinary stealing, so 'never even baked' doesn't show innocence. The punchline needs something like cookies he never touched.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: 'Paul, the baker and I all just heard about that ambush' says Paul knew of the plot. Acts 25 never says Paul knew about it. The line also ties his answer in 25:10-11 to the ambush, which the text never does.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin talks about 'the baker' in the third person while speaking to the baker, instead of talking to them directly.

rule.text: He calls the baker "baker" or "friend," and talks to one baker at a time.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Right where he's standing now' is a casual phrase, while both wrong answers are named places ('In the temple courts', 'Before the Sanhedrin'). That makes the right answer stand out. It also drops the text's key words 'the judgment seat of Caesar,' which set up the appeal.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: 'As Festus himself doubts very well' and 'fears very well' aren't natural English, so 'knows' is the only answer that fits 'very well.' The right answer gives itself away.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: 'Friend, that is not a man ducking anything' is a pleasant remark, not a real laugh, on a moment that could hold one.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: 'And that's where we stop for now, friend, because Paul's story is NOT finished' follows the doc's example line ('And that's where we'll leave it for now. Trust me, friend, this story's not done.') almost word for word, instead of being a fresh line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
